units.sentence: Two lay confessors, neither yet ordained, did write letters to each other that survive in their own words.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Many ordinary people in the countryside spoke a tongue that was not the one we were taught in.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: We do not carry that life in any detail.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: What an ordinary believer felt from inside is not ours to give you.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: The one exception is the tears Augustine shed at his own baptism, which he wrote down years afterward, already a bishop.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: For us, Jesus being God belongs with the Trinity in one confession: we confess Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, our Lord.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Then we confess the Holy Ghost as well, and that completes the Trinity that makes up the one Godhead.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: That confession did not go unchallenged.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: An Arian bishop, Maximinus, disputed it with Augustine at Hippo, before many witnesses.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: At the council of 256, Cyprian stated the rule that no bishop stands over another and each answers to Christ.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Augustine held that small councils yield to wider ones, and that even the widest can later be corrected.

Augustine wrote: “But who does not know this? The holy canon of Scripture, both Old and New Testament, is held within its own limits. It stands far above all later letters of bishops. So no one may doubt or dispute whether what is clearly in it is right and true. But bishops' letters, written since the canon was closed or still being written, may be shown wrong if anything in them strays from the truth. This may come through the word of someone wiser in the matter. It may come through the weightier authority and greater learning of other bishops, or through councils. Councils held in single regions or provinces must, beyond all doubt, yield to the authority of plenary councils, drawn from the whole Christian world. And even among plenary councils, the earlier are often corrected by the later. This happens when some experience of events brings to light what was hidden, and what lay concealed becomes known. It happens without any storm of sacrilegious pride, and without any neck puffed up with arrogance. It happens without any quarrel of envy and hatred. It happens simply with holy humility, catholic peace and Christian love.”

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: The Bible story our record keeps is Paul's thorn, which Augustine taught from when he spoke of prayer that goes unanswered.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Paul asked God three times to take away a thorn in his flesh.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Paul called the thorn a messenger of Satan sent to buffet him.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: God did not take it away.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: God answered instead that his grace was enough for Paul, and that strength is made perfect in weakness.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Augustine taught that Paul was heard for his salvation, though not heard according to his wish.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Augustine made that a rule for the saints, and not for Paul alone.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: They are always heard in what concerns their salvation, even when they are not heard as they wished.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Augustine also told a Manichaean that Moses obeyed God and was not cruel in the wars God commanded.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: The life you ask about is not ours to give you from inside, because what comes down to us is mostly what a bishop saw and decided, not what an ordinary person was feeling.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: We can tell you what was decided about a person, and how carefully, and by whom.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Both of our own voices are bishops.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: No source of ours is written by an ordinary lay believer about ordinary congregational life.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: The preaching our record holds is the bishop's regular talk to the whole gathered church, baptized and still learning.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Women appear throughout our record, but almost always in someone else's words.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Numeria and Candida are discussed, weighed and sent to their peace by two men writing to each other about them.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: We know a woman called Albina, and a community of nuns at Hippo, only through one of our bishop's letters to them and about them.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: From our two cities, in our years from 246 to 430, no text that a woman wrote herself survives.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Now and then a woman's spoken words reach us, set down by men.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: One martyr account gives the vision of Quartillosia, who was held in prison with the martyrs, in her own first person.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: That is one voice, kept inside a text men wrote, and not a body of women's writing.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: What we hold from Augustine's teaching is that Christ's command to turn the other cheek asks for an inward disposition, not a bodily action.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: That teaching does not claim that God never rightly commanded the sword at all.

Augustine wrote: “For many have learned how to offer the other cheek, but do not know how to love the one who strikes them. But in truth the Lord Himself was surely the first to keep the commands He taught. Yet He did not offer the other cheek to the high priest’s servant who struck Him there. Far from it, He said, ‘If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike me?’ Yet He was not, for that reason, unready in heart for the salvation of all. He was ready not only to be struck on the other cheek, but even to have His whole body crucified.”

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Our church gave, and our bishop taught giving: Cyprian wrote a whole treatise on almsgiving, and much of it speaks to believers who had money.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Cyprian told them plainly that their wealth was for sharing their gains with Christ.

units.label: paraphrase
units.sentence: Almsgiving was the ordinary remedy for the sin a person goes on committing after baptism.
Our sayings tell of the ransom of our captive brethren:
Eight bishops wrote to Cyprian, who led our church, that barbarians had carried off our brothers and sisters, and he read their letter with tears.
He answered that we must pay to set them free, not only out of love but because our religion called us to it.
Paul says that everyone baptized into Christ has put on Christ, so we were to see Christ himself in our captive brothers and sisters.
Our clergy and people gave quickly and freely.
We sent the bishops one hundred thousand sesterces to use for the captives as carefully as they could.
